theory.title: HTTP: The Language of the Web
theory.recap: You can route across subnets, pass firewall rules, and navigate multi-hop paths. Now your packet has arrived at the application layer - it carries an actual HTTP request, not just an IP address and port number.
theory.plainObjective: Route through two routers and a firewall, then at the web server choose the path that matches your HTTP method and resource.
theory.summary: HTTP is the protocol browsers and servers use to exchange web content. Every link you click and every image that loads is an HTTP request with a method and a path - and the server's response code tells you exactly what happened.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Methods and paths
bodyParagraphs.text: An HTTP request has two key parts: the method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and the path (/index.html, /api/data). GET means 'give me this resource'. POST means 'here is data to process'. The server decides what to do based on both.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Status codes
bodyParagraphs.text: The server replies with a status code. 200 OK means success. 404 Not Found means the path doesn't exist on this server. 405 Method Not Allowed means the path exists but doesn't accept your method - you tried to POST to a read-only resource.

bodyParagraphs.heading: HTTP is above IP and TCP
bodyParagraphs.text: HTTP runs on top of TCP (which runs on top of IP). By the time an HTTP request arrives at a server, the IP routing and TCP handshake are already complete. HTTP is purely application-layer - the server reads your method and path and decides the response.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Stateless by default
bodyParagraphs.text: HTTP is stateless: each request is independent. The server doesn't remember your previous requests unless something extra (like a cookie or session token) carries state between them. You will see how that works in the next level.

theory.mission:
You carry a GET request for /index.html, destined for 10.50.1.5 on port 80.

Route through R1 and R2, pass the HTTP firewall, reach the web server, then choose the exit that matches your method and resource.

termIntroductions.headline: HTTP Request
termIntroductions.body: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is how browsers and servers talk. Every web request has a method - GET means 'give me this resource'. The path (/index.html) says which resource. Together they form the request line: GET /index.html HTTP/1.1.

termIntroductions.headline: HTTP Response Codes
termIntroductions.body: The server responds with a status code. 200 OK = success. 404 = the path you requested doesn't exist on this server. 405 = path exists but this method isn't allowed. Choose the exit matching your packet: GET /index.html.

termIntroductions.headline: 404 Not Found
termIntroductions.body: The path /secret doesn't exist on this server. The server looked for that resource and couldn't find it. Your packet asked for /index.html - go back and take the correct exit.

termIntroductions.headline: 405 Method Not Allowed
termIntroductions.body: POST /index.html is rejected - this endpoint is read-only and doesn't accept POST. Your packet is a GET request, not POST. Go back and choose the matching path.
